summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is enforced. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Zambian law falls within the conduct the law reaches. Amnesty International's campaign account of 26 November 2024, 'Madalitso's story', describes a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who by November 2024 had served three years of a sentence imposed for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of staff.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, and prolonged detentions of LGBTQI+ people. Advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals, with the fine reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, about $30 to $900. The same report states that the government continued to reject recognition and protection of LGBTQI+ rights.

The 2022 country report found no credible government efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons. It records that police who detain LGBTQI+ people often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release, and that there were no credible reports of government agents condoning violence.

Detention carries the risk of forced anal examination. Human Rights Watch's report of 12 July 2016 documents the practice in at least eight countries including Zambia, where it was less frequent than in Egypt and Tunisia but where prosecutors introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence in sodomy cases, including a mass trial of about 20 men. Victims treated the examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence. Amnesty International described a 2014 case as tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the WHO and medical authorities have condemned the practice.

Societal violence is documented with dates. The most recent instance in the sources is the spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults that followed President Hichilema's statement of 30 May 2022 opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest. In January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Organised opposition has an institutional form: the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts was formed in 1999 to combat homosexuality.

Public advocacy on LGBTQ matters is not permitted. The US State Department's 2021 report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent. In 1998 a vice-president called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona in 2013, an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held that he had reasonably exercised his right to freedom of expression and rejected the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges, and the government contested the decision.

Healthcare access is constrained and only narrowly protected. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, and the 2021 report records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services. Two narrower instruments apply. The Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management on the basis of sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy of 2015 recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human.
tangentialFactors:
Attitude measurement in the sources is historical. A 2010 survey found that 2 percent of Zambians considered homosexuality morally acceptable, nine points below the 11 percent recorded for Uganda in the same survey. The sources describe social attitudes coloured by views of homosexuality as immoral and as a form of insanity, with evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes named as drivers.

One source characterises younger generations as showing slightly more positive and open attitudes toward LGBTQ peers, attributing the shift to internet access and the country's digitisation. That claim carries no survey figure and no date, so its size and currency cannot be assessed.

A statement of a different register exists alongside official hostility: in 2013 Christine Kaseba, spouse of then-President Michael Sata, said that silence around men who have sex with men should end and that no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.
localsOnly:
Discrimination against LGBTQI+ residents in employment, housing, education and health is recorded as continuing in the US State Department's 2021 and 2022 reports, with earlier documentation from 2010 by the same department and by Global Rights and IGLHRC covering access to health care and education.

Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, applies to children who commit gross indecency with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempt to procure such acts. The penalty is such community service or counselling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child. There is no parallel offence for minors of opposite sex.

Registration of LGBTQ organisations is barred in practice. The Registrar of Societies stated in 1998 that he would refuse to register any such organisation, and the government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights.

Most LGBTQ people in Zambia are described as closeted out of fear of targeting, with lesbians identified as especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure. As of July 2007 no public or private programme provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men, adult HIV prevalence stood at about 17 percent, and the government's National AIDS Control Program did not address same-sex relationships. That programme snapshot is historical.
blindOutOfScope:
Whether forced anal examinations continue after the 2016 documentation is unresolved; the latest source on the practice is Human Rights Watch's report of 12 July 2016.

Whether the 2013 freedom-of-expression precedent has been applied in later cases is unresolved. The government contested that decision, and no subsequent case appears in the sources.

No information on trans-specific healthcare or medication appears in the sources. No entry, visa, passport or gender-marker rules for trans travellers are sourced either, and no trans-specific violence count or rate is given against which a general homicide rate could be compared.

The attitude claim about younger generations carries no survey figure and no period, and the 2 percent moral-acceptance figure is a 2010 measurement rather than a current one.
